chunks: Sa'd narrated from Abu Ja'far, from Muhammad ibn Khalid al-Barqi, from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhal, from Marwan ibn Muslim, from Ubayd ibn Zur'ah, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who doubted and did not know whether he had prostrated twice or once, so he prostrated another [prostration], then he became certain that he had added an extra prostration. He said: 'By Allah, the addition of a prostration does not invalidate the prayer.' And he said: 'He does not repeat his prayer from a prostration, but he repeats it from a rak'ah.'
The Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: If he left the tasbih in the ruku' and sujud out of forgetfulness, there is no need for him to repeat the prayer. This is indicated by what he narrated:

key_terms.رَكْعَة: Rak'ah (a unit of prayer consisting of standing, bowing, and prostrating)
key_terms.رُكُوع: Bowings (the act of bowing in prayer)
key_terms.زِيَادَة: Addition/Extra (referring to an additional act in worship)
key_terms.سَجْدَة: Prostration (a specific act of worship in prayer)

ai.seo_question: Does adding an extra prostration due to doubt invalidate the Islamic prayer?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the principle of *istishab* (presumption of continuity) in prayer, affirming that an extra prostration due to doubt does not invalidate the prayer, thereby distinguishing between minor errors in prostration versus major errors in the unit of prayer. Sheikh al-Tusi’s commentary highlights the leniency in Shia jurisprudence, noting that omitting recommended remembrances (*tasbih*) out of forgetfulness does not necessitate re-praying, reflecting the broader theological emphasis on ease (*yusr*) in worship. This ruling is foundational for understanding how Shia scholars handle *shakk* (doubt) in the daily *salat*, prioritizing the validity of the act over perfection of detail.
